audioscript.text: Part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a man phoning to find out about some children's engineering workshops.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 3.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 3.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Hello, children's engineering workshops.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: Oh, hello.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: I wanted some information about the workshops in the school holidays.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: Sure.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: I have two daughters who are interested.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: The younger one's Lydia.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: She's 4.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: Do you take children as young as that?
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: Yes, our Tiny Engineers workshop is for 4 to 5 year olds.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: What sorts of activities do they do?
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: All sorts.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: For example, they work together to design a special cover that goes round an egg, so that when it's inside, they can drop it from a height, and it doesn't break.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH
audioscript.explain: Q1: The passage says they design a cover that goes round *'an egg'* so it doesn't break when dropped. The question asks what the cover is for — it's for an **egg**. So the answer is **egg**.

audioscript.text: Well, sometimes it does break, but that's part of the fun.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: And Lydia loves building things.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: Is there any opportunity for her to do that?
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: Well, they have a competition to see who can make the highest tower.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH
audioscript.explain: Q2: The passage says they have a competition to make the *'highest tower'* — **'highest'** means the same as **'tallest'** in the question. So the answer is **tower**.

audioscript.text: You'd be amazed how high they can go.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: But they're learning all the time as well as having fun.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: For example, one thing they do is to design and build a car that's attached to a balloon.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH
audioscript.explain: Q3: The passage says they design and build *'a car that's attached to a balloon'* — the balloon's air powers it. The question asks what they make that is **powered by a balloon** — it's a **car**. So the answer is **car**.

audioscript.text: And the force of the air in that actually powers the car, and makes it move along.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: They go really fast too.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: OK, well, all this sounds perfect.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 4 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 4 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now Carly, that's my older daughter, has just had her 7th birthday.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: So presumably she'd be in a different group.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: Yes.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: She'd be in the Junior Engineers.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: That's for children from 6 to 8.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: And do they do the same sorts of activities?
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: Some are the same.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: But a bit more advanced.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: So they work out how to build model vehicles, things like cars and trucks, but also how to construct animals using the same sorts of material and technique.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH
audioscript.explain: Q4: The passage says Junior Engineers build model vehicles like cars and trucks, but also *'construct animals'* using the same materials. The question lists cars, trucks and asks for the third thing — it's **animals**. So the answer is **animals**.

audioscript.text: And then they learn how they can program them and make them move.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: So they learn a bit of coding.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: They do.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: They pick it up really quickly.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: We're there to help if they need it, but they learn from one another too.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: And do they have competitions too?
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: Yes, with the Junior Engineers, it's to use recycled materials like card and wood.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH
audioscript.explain: Q5: The passage says the competition is to use card and wood to *'build a bridge, and the longest one gets a prize'*. The question asks what they build the longest of — it's a **bridge**. So the answer is **bridge**.

audioscript.text: To build a bridge, and the longest one gets a prize.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH
audioscript.explain: Q5: The passage says the competition is to use card and wood to *'build a bridge, and the longest one gets a prize'*. The question asks what they build the longest of — it's a **bridge**. So the answer is **bridge**.

audioscript.text: That sounds fun, I wouldn't mind doing that myself.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: Then they have something a bit different.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: Which is to think up an idea for a 5 minute movie, and then film it using special animation software.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH
audioscript.explain: Q6: The passage says they think up an idea for a *'5 minute movie'* and film it — **'movie'** is the same as **'film'** here. The question asks what short thing they create — it's a **movie** or **film**. So the answer is **movie** or **film**.

audioscript.text: You'd be amazed what they come up with.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: And of course that's something they can put on their phone,
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: and take home to show all their friends.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: Exactly.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: And then they also build a robot in the shape of a human, and they decorate it and program it so that it can move its arms and legs.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH
audioscript.explain: Q7: The passage says they build a human-shaped robot and *'decorate it and program it'* to move. The question has blanks for build, ___ and program — the missing word is **decorate**. So the answer is **decorate**.

audioscript.text: Perfect.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: So is it the same price as the tiny engineers?
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: It's just a bit more, £50 for the 5 weeks.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: And are the classes on a Monday too?
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: They used to be, but we found it didn't give our staff enough time to clear up after the first workshop, so we moved them to Wednesdays.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH
audioscript.explain: Q8: The passage says they moved the classes from Monday to *'Wednesdays'* because staff needed more time. The question asks what day the classes are held — it's **Wednesdays**. So the answer is **Wednesdays**.

audioscript.text: The classes are held in the morning from 10 to 11.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: OK, that's better for me actually.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: And what about the location?
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: Where exactly are the workshops held?
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: They're in building 10A.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: There's a big sign on the door, you can't miss it.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: And that's in Fradstone Industrial Estate.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH
audioscript.explain: Q9: The passage says the location is building 10A in *'Fradstone Industrial Estate'*. The question asks for the name of the industrial estate — it's **Fradstone**. So the answer is **Fradstone**.

audioscript.text: Sorry?
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: Fradstone.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: That's FRADSTONE.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: And that's in Grasford, isn't it?
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: Yes, up past the station.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: And will I have any parking problems there?
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: No, there's always plenty available.
audioscript.speaker: SARAH
audioscript.explain: Q10: The man asks about parking problems and the reply is *'there's always plenty available'* — **'plenty available'** means lots of **parking**. The question says plenty of what is available — it's **parking**. So the answer is **parking**.

audioscript.text: So would you like to enroll Lydia and Carly now?
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: OK.
audioscript.speaker: FATHER

audioscript.text: So can I have your full name?
audioscript.speaker: SARAH

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Part 2, you will hear the Managing Director of a company called Stevenson's welcoming a group of work experience students.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Good morning everyone, and welcome to Stevenson's, one of the country's major manufacturers of metal goods.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: Thank you for choosing us for your two weeks of work experience.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: My name is Julia Simmons, and since the beginning of this year, I've been the managing director.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: Stevenson's is quite an old company.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: Like me, the founder Ronald Stevenson went into the steel industry when he left school.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: That was in 1923.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: He set up this company when he finished his apprenticeship, in 1926, although he actually started making plans two years earlier, in 1924. He was a very determined young man!
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS
audioscript.explain: Q11: The passage says *'He set up this company when he finished his apprenticeship, in 1926'* — **'set up'** means **'founded'**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: Stevenson's long-term plan was to manufacture components for the machine tools industry, although in fact that never came about, and for the automotive industry, that is, cars and lorries.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: However, there was a delay of five years before that happened.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: Because shortly before the company went into production, Stevenson was given the opportunity to make goods for hospitals.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says *'Stevenson was given the opportunity to make goods for hospitals'* and *'other players in the health care industry'* — **'health care industry'** is the same as **'healthcare industry'**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: And other players in the health care industry, so that's what we did for the first five years.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says *'Stevenson was given the opportunity to make goods for hospitals'* and *'other players in the health care industry'* — **'health care industry'** is the same as **'healthcare industry'**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Over the years, we've expanded the premises considerably.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: We were lucky that the site is big enough, so moving to a new location has never been necessary.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS
audioscript.explain: Q13: The passage says *'moving to a new location has never been necessary'* — this means the company has **no plans to move**. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: However, the layout is far from ideal for modern machinery and production methods, so we intend to carry out major refurbishment of this site over the next five years.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: I'd better give you some idea of what you'll be doing during your two weeks with us, so you know what to expect.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: Most mornings you'll have a presentation from one of the managers.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS
audioscript.explain: Q14: The passage says *'Most mornings you'll have a presentation from one of the managers'* — a **'presentation'** is a **'talk'**, and **'managers'** are **'staff'**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: To learn about their department, starting this morning with research and development.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: And you'll all spend some time in each department, observing what's going on and talking to people,
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: as long as you don't stop them from doing their work altogether! In the past, a teacher from your school has come in at the end of each week to find out how the group were getting on.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: But your school isn't able to arrange that this year.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: OK, now I'll briefly help you to orientate yourselves around the site.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: As you can see, we're in the reception area, which we try to make attractive and welcoming to visitors.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: There's a corridor running left from here, and if you go along that, the door facing you at the end is the entrance to the coffee room.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS
audioscript.explain: Q15: The passage says *'the door facing you at the end is the entrance to the coffee room'* — you go left from reception to the end of the corridor. On the map, that is **H**.

audioscript.text: This looks out onto the main road on one side, and some trees on the other.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

audioscript.text: And that'll be where you meet each morning.
audioscript.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS
audioscript.explain: Q15: The passage says *'the door facing you at the end is the entrance to the coffee room'* — you go left from reception to the end of the corridor. On the map, that is **H**.

audioscript.text: Part 4, you will hear a professor of philosophy giving a talk on the ancient philosophy of Stoicism.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Ancient philosophy is not just about talking or lecturing, or even reading long dense books.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In fact, it is something people have used throughout history.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: To solve their problems and to achieve their greatest triumphs.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Specifically, I am referring to Stoicism, which in my opinion is the most practical of all philosophies, and therefore the most appealing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says Stoicism is *'the most practical of all philosophies, and therefore the most appealing'*. The question asks why Stoicism is still relevant — it's because of its **'practical'** appeal. So the answer is **practical**.

audioscript.text: Stoicism was founded in ancient Greece by Zeno of Citium in the early 3rd century BC, but was practiced by the likes of Epictetus.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Cato, Seneca, and Marcus Aurelius.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Amazingly, we still have access to these ideas, despite the fact that the most famous Stoics never wrote anything down for publication.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says the most famous Stoics *'never wrote anything down for publication'*. The question says their ideas were not intended for something — that something is **'publication'**. So the answer is **publication**.

audioscript.text: Cato definitely didn't, Marcus Aurelius never intended his Meditations to be anything but personal, Seneca's letters were, well, letters.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And Epictetus' thoughts come to us by way of a note-taking student.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Stoic principles were based on the idea that its followers could have an unshakable happiness in this life, and the key to achieving this was virtue.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The road to virtue in turn lay in understanding that destructive emotions like anger and jealousy are under our conscious control.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They don't have to control us, because we can learn to control them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In the words of Epictetus, external events I cannot control, but the choices I make with regard to them, I do control.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: Epictetus said *'external events I cannot control, but the choices I make with regard to them, I do control'*. The question uses the same idea — external events can't be controlled, but the **'choices'** people make can. So the answer is **choices**.

audioscript.text: The modern day philosopher and writer, Nassim Nicholas Taleb, defines a Stoic as someone who has a different perspective on experiences,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage defines a Stoic as someone with a different view on experiences *'which most of us would see as wholly negative'*. The question asks what others would consider these experiences — they would see them as **'negative'**. So the answer is **negative**.

audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage defines a Stoic as someone with a different view on experiences *'which most of us would see as wholly negative'*. The question asks what others would consider these experiences — they would see them as **'negative'**. So the answer is **negative**.

audioscript.text: A Stoic "transforms fear into caution, pain into transformation, mistakes into initiation, and desire into undertaking". Using this definition as a model, we can see that throughout the centuries Stoicism has been practiced in more recent history by kings.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Presidents, artists, writers, and entrepreneurs.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The founding fathers of the United States were inspired by the philosophy.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: George Washington was introduced to Stoicism by his neighbors at age 17.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And later put on a play based on the life of Cato to inspire his men.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says George Washington *'put on a play based on the life of Cato to inspire his men'*. The question says he organised a something about Cato to motivate — that something is a **'play'**. So the answer is **play**.

audioscript.text: Thomas Jefferson kept a copy of Seneca beside his bed.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Writers and artists have also been inspired by the Stoics, Eugène Delacroix, the renowned French Romantic artist, known best for his painting Liberty Leading the People, was an ardent Stoic, referring to it as his consoling religion.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The economist Adam Smith's theories on capitalism were significantly influenced by the Stoicism that he studied as a schoolboy, under a teacher who had translated Marcus Aurelius' works.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says *'Adam Smith's theories on capitalism were significantly influenced by the Stoicism'*. The question asks what ideas were influenced — his ideas on **'capitalism'**. So the answer is **capitalism**.

audioscript.text: Today's political leaders are no different, with many finding their inspiration from the ancient texts.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Former US President Bill Clinton rereads Marcus Aurelius every single year, and many have compared former President Obama's calm leadership style to that of Cato.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Wen Jiabao, the former prime minister of China, claims that Meditations is one of two books he travels with, and that he has read it more than 100 times over the course of his life.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Stoicism had a profound influence on Albert Ellis, who invented cognitive behavior therapy, which is used to help people manage their problems,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: by changing the way that they think and behave.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's most commonly used to treat depression.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says Cognitive Behaviour Therapy *'is most commonly used to treat depression'*. The question asks what the treatment is for — it is for **'depression'**. So the answer is **depression**.

audioscript.text: The idea is that we can take control of our lives by challenging the irrational beliefs
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: that create our faulty thinking symptoms and behaviors by using logic instead.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says people can change faulty thinking *'by using logic instead'*. The question says people learn to base their thinking on something — that something is **'logic'**. So the answer is **logic**.

audioscript.text: Stoicism has also become popular in the world of business.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Stoic principles can build the resilience and state of mind required to overcome setbacks, because Stoics teach turning obstacles into opportunity.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says Stoics teach *'turning obstacles into opportunity'*. The question says people benefit by identifying obstacles as something — that something is **'opportunity'**. So the answer is **opportunity**.

audioscript.text: A lesson every business entrepreneur needs to learn.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I would argue that studying Stoicism is as relevant today as it was 2,000 years ago, thanks to its brilliant insights into how to lead a good life.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: At the very root of the thinking, there is a very simple way of living.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Control what you can, and accept what you can't.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is not as easy as it sounds, and will require considerable practice.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says Stoicism *'will require considerable practice'*. The question says it requires a lot of something — that something is **'practice'** (or **'practise'**). So the answer is **practice**.

audioscript.text: It can take a lifetime to master.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The Stoics also believed the most important foundation for a good and happy life is not money, fame, power or pleasure, but having a disciplined and principled character.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Something which seems to resonate with many people today.

utterances.text: Stoicism was founded in ancient Greece by Zeno of Citium in the early 3rd century BC, but was practiced by the likes of Epictetus.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Cato, Seneca, and Marcus Aurelius.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Amazingly, we still have access to these ideas, despite the fact that the most famous Stoics never wrote anything down for publication.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q32: The passage says the most famous Stoics *'never wrote anything down for publication'*. The question says their ideas were not intended for something — that something is **'publication'**. So the answer is **publication**.

utterances.text: Cato definitely didn't, Marcus Aurelius never intended his Meditations to be anything but personal, Seneca's letters were, well, letters.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: And Epictetus' thoughts come to us by way of a note-taking student.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Stoic principles were based on the idea that its followers could have an unshakable happiness in this life, and the key to achieving this was virtue.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: The road to virtue in turn lay in understanding that destructive emotions like anger and jealousy are under our conscious control.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: They don't have to control us, because we can learn to control them.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: The modern day philosopher and writer, Nassim Nicholas Taleb, defines a Stoic as someone who has a different perspective on experiences,

utterances.text: Writers and artists have also been inspired by the Stoics, Eugène Delacroix, the renowned French Romantic artist, known best for his painting Liberty Leading the People, was an ardent Stoic, referring to it as his consoling religion.

utterances.text: Today's political leaders are no different, with many finding their inspiration from the ancient texts.

utterances.text: Former US President Bill Clinton rereads Marcus Aurelius every single year, and many have compared former President Obama's calm leadership style to that of Cato.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Wen Jiabao, the former prime minister of China, claims that Meditations is one of two books he travels with, and that he has read it more than 100 times over the course of his life.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Stoicism had a profound influence on Albert Ellis, who invented cognitive behavior therapy, which is used to help people manage their problems,

utterances.text: by changing the way that they think and behave.

utterances.text: The idea is that we can take control of our lives by challenging the irrational beliefs
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: that create our faulty thinking symptoms and behaviors by using logic instead.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q38: The passage says people can change faulty thinking *'by using logic instead'*. The question says people learn to base their thinking on something — that something is **'logic'**. So the answer is **logic**.

utterances.text: Stoicism has also become popular in the world of business.

utterances.text: Stoic principles can build the resilience and state of mind required to overcome setbacks, because Stoics teach turning obstacles into opportunity.

utterances.text: A lesson every business entrepreneur needs to learn.

utterances.text: I would argue that studying Stoicism is as relevant today as it was 2,000 years ago, thanks to its brilliant insights into how to lead a good life.

utterances.text: At the very root of the thinking, there is a very simple way of living.

audioscript.text: Part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a woman phoning a company that converts old photographs to digital format.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 3.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 3.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Hello, Picturerep.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: Can I help you?
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: Oh, hi.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: I saw your advertisement about copying pictures to disk, and I'd like a bit more information about what you do.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Sure, what would you like to know?
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: Well, I've got a box full of old family photos that's been up in the attic for years.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Some of them must be 50 or 60 years old.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: And I'd like to get them converted to digital format.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Sure, we can do that for you.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: Right, and what about size?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: The photos are all sorts of sizes.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Are there any restrictions?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Well, the maximum size of photo we can do with our normal service is 30 centimeters, and each picture must be at least 4 cm.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: That's the minimum we can cope with.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: Oh, that should be fine.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: And some of them are in a frame.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN
audioscript.explain: Q1: The question asks what photos must NOT be in. The woman asks *'Should I take them out before I send them?'* about photos in a **frame**, and the company says *'Yes, please'*. So the answer is **frame**.

audioscript.text: Should I take them out before I send them?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Yes, please.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: We can't copy them otherwise, and also the photos must all be separate, they mustn't be stuck into an album.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: OK, that's not a problem.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: So, can you give me an idea of how much this will cost?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: I've got about 360 photos, I think.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: We charge £195 for 300 to 400 photos for the basic service.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE
audioscript.explain: Q2: The woman says she has *'about 360 photos'*. The company replies *'We charge £195 for 300 to 400 photos'*. So the cost for 360 photos is **195**.

audioscript.text: OK, and does that include the disk?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Yes, one disk, but you can get extra ones for £5 each.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: That's good.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: So, do I need to pay when I send you the photos?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: No, we won't need anything until we've actually copied the pictures.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: Then we'll let you know how much it is, and once we've received the payment, we'll send the parcel off to you.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE
audioscript.explain: Q3: The question asks what is required before the order is sent. The company says *'once we've received the payment, we'll send the parcel off to you'*. So **payment** is needed first.

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 4 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 4 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Is there anything else you'd like to ask about our services?
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: Yes, I've roughly sorted out the photos into groups according to what they're about.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: So, can you keep them in those groups when you copy them?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Sure, we'll save each group in a different folder on the disk, and if you like, you can suggest a name for each folder.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: So, I could have one called 'Grandparents' for instance?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN
audioscript.explain: Q4: The question asks for an example of a folder name. The woman suggests *'one called 'Grandparents' for instance'*, and the company agrees. So the answer is **Grandparents**.

audioscript.text: Exactly.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: And do you do anything besides scan the photos?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Like, can you make any improvements?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Yes, in the standard service, each photo is checked, and we can sometimes touch up the color a bit, or improve the contrast,
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE
audioscript.explain: Q5: The question asks what can be improved besides contrast. The passage says they can *'touch up the color a bit, or improve the contrast'*. So the answer is **colour** or **color**.

audioscript.text: that can make a big difference.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: OK, and some of the photos are actually quite fragile.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: They won't get damaged in the process, will they?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: No, if any look particularly fragile, we'd do them by hand.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE
audioscript.explain: Q6: The question asks how fragile photos are scanned. The company says *'if any look particularly fragile, we'd do them by hand'*. So the answer is **hand**.

audioscript.text: We do realize how precious these old photos can be.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: Sure.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: And another thing is we can make changes to a photo if you want,
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: so, if you want to remove an object from a photo, or maybe alter the background,
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE
audioscript.explain: Q7: The question asks what can be changed in the special restore service. The passage says you can *'remove an object from a photo, or maybe alter the background'*. So the answer is **background**.

audioscript.text: we can do that.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: Really?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: I might be interested in that.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: I'll have a look through the photos and see.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Oh, and talking of fixing photos.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: I've got a few that aren't properly in focus.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN
audioscript.explain: Q8: The question asks what cannot be fixed if it is not correct. The woman says some photos *'aren't properly in focus'*, and the company says *'that's one thing we can't do'*. So the answer is **focus**.

audioscript.text: Can you do anything to make that better?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: No, I'm afraid that's one thing we can't do.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: OK.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Any other information I can give you?
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: Er... oh, how long will it all take?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: We aim to get the copying done in 10 days.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE
audioscript.explain: Q9: The question asks how long orders take. The company says *'We aim to get the copying done in 10 days'*. So the answer is **10 days** or **ten days**.

audioscript.text: Fine.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Right, well, I'll get the photos packed up in a box and post them off to you.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Right, if you've got a strong cardboard box, that's best.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: We've found that plastic ones sometimes break in the post.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE
audioscript.explain: Q10: The question asks what type of box NOT to use. The company says *'plastic ones sometimes break in the post'*, so a **plastic** box is not good.

audioscript.text: OK.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Right, thanks for your help.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Bye.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Bye.
audioscript.speaker: EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: So, Luke, for our next psychology assignment, we have to do something on sleep and dreams.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: I've just read an article suggesting why we tend to forget most of our dreams soon after we wake up.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: I mean most of my dreams aren't that interesting anyway, but what it said was that if we remembered everything, we might get mixed up about what actually happened.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE
audioscript.explain: Q21: The passage says if we remembered all dreams, we might get *'mixed up about what actually happened'* — **'mixed up'** means **'confused'**. So the worry is we would be **confused about what is real**. The answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: And what we dreamed, so it's a sort of protection.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: I hadn't heard that idea before.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: I'd always assumed that it was just that we didn't have room in our memories for all that stuff.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: Me too.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: What do you think about the idea that our dreams may predict the future?
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: It's a belief that you get all over the world.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: Yeah, lots of people have a story of it happening to them.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: But the explanation I've read is that for each dream that comes true, we have thousands that don't.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: But we don't notice those, we don't even remember them.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: We just remember the ones where something in the real world, like a view or an action happens to trigger a dream memory.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: So it's just a coincidence really.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE
audioscript.explain: Q22: Luke says the explanation is that for every dream that comes true, thousands don't, and we only remember the ones that match real life. audioscript.text: Hmm.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: Something else I read about is what they call segmented sleeping.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: That's a theory that hundreds of years ago, people used to get up in the middle of the night, and have a chat or something to eat.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: Then go back to bed.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: So I tried it myself.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: Why?
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: Well, it's meant to make you more creative.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: I don't know why, but I gave it up after a week,
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: it just didn't fit in with my lifestyle.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: But most preschool children have a short sleep in the day, don't they?
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: There was an experiment some students did here last term.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: To see at what age kids should stop having naps, but they didn't really find an answer.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: Last time, I had problems with the final stage.
audioscript.speaker: LUKE

audioscript.text: Dancing is something that humans do when they want to have a good time.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's a universal response to music found in all cultures. But what's only been discovered recently,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: is that dancing not only makes us feel good, it's also extremely good for our health.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Dancing, like other forms of exercise, releases hormones.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Such as dopamine, which make us feel relaxed and happy, and it also reduces feelings of stress or anxiety.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Dancing is also a sociable activity, which is another reason it makes us feel good.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One study compared people's enjoyment of dancing at home, in front of a video.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: With dancing in a group in a studio.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The people dancing in a group reported feeling happier, whereas those dancing alone did not.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In another experiment, university researchers at York and Sheffield took a group of students and sent each of them into a lab where music was played for five minutes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Each had to choose from three options, to sit and listen quietly to the music, to cycle on an exercise bike while they listened.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Or to get up and dance.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: All were given cognitive tasks to perform before and after.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The result showed that those who chose to dance showed much more creativity.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says those who danced showed *'much more creativity'* when solving problems. The question asks what dance increases, and **'creativity'** is the direct answer.

audioscript.text: When doing problem solving tasks.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says those who danced showed *'much more creativity'* when solving problems. The question asks what dance increases, and **'creativity'** is the direct answer.

audioscript.text: Doctor Lovatt, at the University of Hertfordshire, believes dance could be a very useful way to help people suffering from mental health problems.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He thinks dance should be prescribed as therapy to help people overcome issues such as depression.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says dance should be *'prescribed as therapy'* for mental health issues. **'Prescribed as'** means used as a form of, so the answer is **'therapy'**.

audioscript.text: It's well established that dance is a good way of encouraging adolescent girls to take exercise, but what about older people?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Studies have shown that there are enormous benefits for people in their 60s and beyond.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One of the great things about dance is that there are no barriers to participation.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Anyone can have a go, even those whose standard of fitness is quite low.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says *'even those whose standard of fitness is quite low'* can dance. **'Standard of fitness'** means level of fitness, so the answer is **'fitness'**.

audioscript.text: Dance can be especially beneficial for older adults who can't run or do more intense workouts, or for those who don't want to.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One 2015 study found that even a gentle dance workout helps to promote a healthy heart.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And there's plenty of evidence which suggests that dancing lowers the risk of falls.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says dancing lowers fall risk by *'helping people to improve their balance'*. Better **'balance'** reduces accidents, so the answer is **'balance'**.

audioscript.text: Which could result in a broken hip for example, by helping people to improve their balance.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says dancing lowers fall risk by *'helping people to improve their balance'*. Better **'balance'** reduces accidents, so the answer is **'balance'**.

audioscript.text: There are some less obvious benefits of dance for older people too.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One thing I hadn't realized before researching this topic was that dance isn't just a physical challenge.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It also requires a lot of concentration, because you need to remember different steps and routines.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For older people, this kind of activity is especially important.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says dance *'forces their brain to process things more quickly'*. The question asks what function improves, and **'brain'** is the answer.

audioscript.text: Because it forces their brain to process things more quickly, and to retain more information.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says dance *'forces their brain to process things more quickly'*. The question asks what function improves, and **'brain'** is the answer.

audioscript.text: Current research also shows that dance promotes a general sense of well-being in older participants, which can last up to a week after a class.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Participants report feeling less tired, and having greater motivation to be more active, and do daily activities such as gardening.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says participants have *'greater motivation to be more active'*. This gives people more **'motivation'** to exercise, so the answer is **'motivation'**.

audioscript.text: Or walking to the shops or a park.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Ballroom or country dancing, both popular with older people, have to be done in groups.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They require collaboration, and often involve touching a dance partner.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: All of which encourages interaction on the dance floor.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This helps to develop new relationships, and can reduce older people's sense of isolation.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says dance can *'reduce older people's sense of isolation'*. Lessening a feeling of **'isolation'** matches the question, so the answer is **'isolation'**.

audioscript.text: Which is a huge problem in many countries.

audioscript.text: An aerobic workout based on Latin American dance moves, John Porcari, a professor of exercise and sport science at the University of Wisconsin,

audioscript.text: A study in the American Journal of Health Behavior showed that when women with obesity did Zumba three times a week for 16 weeks.

audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says the study involved *'women with obesity'*. The question asks who benefited, and **'obesity'** is the condition, so the answer is **'obesity'**.

audioscript.text: That they made it a habit, and continued to attend classes at least once a week, very unusual for an aerobic exercise program.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says women *'made it a habit'* to attend Zumba classes. Zumba became a **'habit'** for them, so the answer is **'habit'**.

body.title: JUNIOR CYCLE CAMP

audioscript.text: Part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a woman phoning to ask about a summer cycling camp for her young son, who is called Charlie.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Hello, Junior Cycle Camp, Jake speaking.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Hi.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: I'm calling for some information about the cycle camp.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: I'm thinking of sending my son.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Great.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Well, it's held every weekday morning over the summer vacation.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: And we focus on basic cycling skills and safety.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: We have eight levels for children from 3 years upwards.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: How old's your son?
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Charlie, he's 7.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: He can ride a bike, but he needs a little more training before he's safe to go on the road.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: He'd probably be best in level 5.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: They start off practicing on the site here, and we aim to get them riding on the road.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: But first, they're taken to ride in the park, away from the traffic.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE
audioscript.explain: Q1: The passage says *'they're taken to ride in the park'* — this is the first place children at Level 5 practice. So the answer is **park**.

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: And can you tell me a bit about the instructors?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Well, all our staff wear different colored shirts.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: So we have three supervisors, and they have red shirts.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: They support the instructors, and they also stand in for me if I'm not around.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Then the instructors themselves are in blue shirts.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE
audioscript.explain: Q2: The passage directly states *'the instructors themselves are in blue shirts'*. So the answer is **blue**.

audioscript.text: And one of these is responsible for each class.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: OK.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: In order to be accepted, all our instructors have to submit a reference from someone who's seen them work with children.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE
audioscript.explain: Q3: The passage says instructors must *'submit a reference'* to be accepted. So the answer is **reference**.

audioscript.text: Like if they've worked as a babysitter for example.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Then they have to complete our training course, including how to do lesson plans, and generally care for the well-being of the kids in their class.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: They do a great job, I have to say.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Right, and tell me a bit about the classes.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: What size will Charlie's class be?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: We have a limit of 8 children in each class, so their instructor really gets to know them well.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: They're out riding most of the time.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: But they have quiet times too, where their instructor might tell them a story that's got something to do with cycling.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE
audioscript.explain: Q4: The passage mentions quiet times include *'a story'* or a game. So the answer is **story**.

audioscript.text: Or get them to play a game together.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: It's a lot of fun.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: It must be.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: What happens if there's rain?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Do the classes still run?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Oh yes, we don't let that put us off.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE
audioscript.explain: Q5: The woman asks about rain, and the man says *'we don't let that put us off'* — meaning classes still happen. So the answer is **rain**.

audioscript.text: We just put on our waterproofs.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: And keep cycling.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: And is there anything special Charlie should bring along with him?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Well, maybe some spare clothes, especially if the weather's not so good.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: A snack for break time.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE
audioscript.explain: Q6: The passage lists what to bring, including *'A snack for break time'*. So the answer is **snack**.

audioscript.text: How about a drink?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: No, we'll provide that.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: And make sure he has shoes, not sandals.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Sure.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: And just at present, Charlie has to take medication every few hours, so I'll make sure he has that.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN
audioscript.explain: Q7: The mother says Charlie *'has to take medication'*, so she will bring it. So the answer is **medication**.

audioscript.text: Absolutely.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Just give us details of when he has to take it, and we'll make sure he does.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Thanks.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Now, there are a few things you should know about day one of the camp.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: The classes normally start at 9:30 every morning, but on day one, you should aim to get Charlie here by 9:20.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: The finishing time will be 12:30 as usual.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: We need the additional time because there are a few extra things to do.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: The most important is that we have a very careful check to make sure that every child's helmet fits properly.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE
audioscript.explain: Q8: On day one, they check that every child's *'helmet fits properly'*. So the answer is **helmet**.

audioscript.text: If it doesn't fit, we'll try to adjust it, or we'll find him another one.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: But he must wear it all the time he's on the bike.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Of course.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Then after that, all the instructors will be waiting to meet their classes, and they'll meet up in the tent.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE
audioscript.explain: Q9: After the helmet check, instructors and classes *'meet up in the tent'*. So the answer is **tent**.

audioscript.text: You can't miss it.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Each instructor will take their class away and get started.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: OK, well that all sounds good.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Now, can you tell me how much the camp costs a week?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN
JAKE
audioscript.explain: Q10: The man says the camp costs *'$199'* per week. So the answer is **199**.

audioscript.text: We've managed to keep the price more or less the same as last year.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: It was 190 then.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: But the places are filling up quite quickly.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: OK, well, I'd like to book for the...
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Hello, everyone.
audioscript.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

audioscript.text: My name is Megan Baker, and I'm a recruitment consultant at AVT Recruitment Specialists.
audioscript.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

audioscript.text: Now, our company specializes in positions that involve working in the agriculture and horticulture sectors, so that's fresh food production.
audioscript.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

audioscript.text: Garden and park maintenance and so on, and these sectors do provide some very special career opportunities.
audioscript.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

audioscript.text: For a start, they often offer opportunities for those who don't want to be stuck with a 40 hour week, but need to juggle work with other responsibilities, such as childcare.

audioscript.text: Part 4, you will hear a lecturer on a fashion design course introducing the subject of hand knitting, which involves making things like woolen jumpers and scarves.

audioscript.text: Good morning everyone, so today we're going to look at an important creative activity, and that's hand knitting.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Ancient knitted garments have been found in many different countries.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Showing that knitting is a global activity with a long history.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: When someone says the word knitting, we might well picture an elderly person.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A grandmother perhaps, sitting by the fire, knitting garments for herself or other members of the family.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says *'A grandmother perhaps, sitting by the fire, knitting garments'* — this is the exact image the question asks for. So the answer is **grandmother**.

audioscript.text: It's a homely image.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But one that may lead you to feel that knitting is an activity of the past, and indeed during the previous decade, it was one of the skills that was predicted to vanish from everyday life.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says *'during the previous decade, it was one of the skills that was predicted to vanish'* — **'previous decade'** means a period of ten years ago. So the answer is **decade**.

audioscript.text: For although humans have sewn and knitted their own clothing for a very long time, many of these craft-based skills went into decline.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: When industrial machines took over, mainly because they were no longer passed down from one generation to another.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: However, that's all changing, and interest in knitting classes in many countries is actually rising.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As more and more people are seeking formal instruction in the skill. With that trend, we're also seeing an increase in the sales figures,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says *'an increase in the sales figures, for knitting equipment'* — **'sales figures'** means people are buying more. So the answer is **equipment**.

audioscript.text: for knitting equipment.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says *'an increase in the sales figures, for knitting equipment'* — **'sales figures'** means people are buying more. So the answer is **equipment**.

audioscript.text: So, why do people want to be taught to knit at a time when a machine can readily do the job for them?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The answer is that knitting as a handicraft has numerous benefits for those doing it.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Let's consider what some of these might be.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: While many people knitted garments in the past, because they couldn't afford to buy clothes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's still true today that knitting can be helpful, if you're experiencing economic hardship.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says knitting helps *'if you're experiencing economic hardship'* — **'hardship'** means **difficulty**. So the answer is **economic**.

audioscript.text: If you have several children who all need warm winter clothes, knitting may save you a lot of money. And the results of knitting your own clothes, can be very rewarding,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: even though the skills you need to get going are really quite basic, and the financial outlay is minimal.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says *'the skills you need to get going are really quite basic'* — **'quite basic'** means they are simple and not advanced. So the answer is **basic**.

audioscript.text: But the more significant benefits in today's world are to do with well-being.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In a world where it's estimated that we spend up to nine hours a day online.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Doing something with our hands that is craft based makes us feel good.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It releases us from the stress of a technological fast paced life.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Now, let's look back a bit to early knitting activities.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In fact, no one really knows when knitting first began.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But archaeological remains have disclosed plenty of information for us to think about.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One of the interesting things about knitting is that the earliest pieces of clothing that have been found suggest that most of the items produced were round rather than flat.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says *'most of the items produced were round rather than flat'* — this directly tells us the shape of early knitted items. So the answer is **round**.

audioscript.text: Discoveries from the 3rd and 4th centuries in Egypt show that things like socks and gloves that were needed to keep hands and feet warm were knitted in one piece using four or five needles.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That's very different.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: From most knitting patterns today, which only require two.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: What's more, the very first needles people used were hand carved out of wood.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says first needles were *'hand carved out of wood'* and *'other natural materials like bone'* — **'like'** gives an example. So the answer is **bone**.

audioscript.text: And other natural materials like bone, whereas today's needles are largely made of steel or plastic, and make that characteristic clicking sound.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says first needles were *'hand carved out of wood'* and *'other natural materials like bone'* — **'like'** gives an example. So the answer is **bone**.

audioscript.text: When someone's using them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Ancient people knitted using yarns made from linen, hemp, cotton, and wool.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And these were often very rough on the skin.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says early yarns *'were often very rough on the skin'* — **'rough on the skin'** means they felt unpleasant to touch. So the answer is **rough**.

audioscript.text: The spinning wheel, which allowed people to make finer yarns, and produce much greater quantities of them, led to the dominance of wool in the knitting industry.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Wool was often favored for its warmth.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Another interesting fact about knitting is that because it was practiced in so many parts of the world, for so many purposes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Regional differences in style developed.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says *'Regional differences in style developed'* — **'regional differences'** means each geographical area had its own way. So the answer is **style**.

audioscript.text: This visual identity has allowed researchers to match bits of knitted clothing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That have been unearthed over time to the region from which the wearer came, or the job that he or she did.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As I've mentioned, knitting offered people from poor communities a way of making extra money while doing other tasks.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For many centuries, it seems, men, women and children took every opportunity to knit, for example, while watching over sheep, walking to market.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says people knitted *'while watching over sheep'* — **'watching over'** means **looking after**. So the answer is **sheep**.

audioscript.text: Or riding in boats.

utterances.text: Let's consider what some of these might be.

utterances.text: It's still true today that knitting can be helpful, if you're experiencing economic hardship.

audioscript.text: Part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a man phoning the owner of a holiday cottage.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Hello?
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: Oh hello.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: I was hoping to speak to Jack Fitzgerald about renting a cottage.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: I'm his wife Shirley, and we own the cottages together, so I'm sure I can help you.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: Great, my name's Tom.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Some friends of ours rented Granary Cottage from you last year, and they thought it was great.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: So my wife and I are hoping to come in May for a week.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: What date did you have in mind?
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: The week beginning the 14th, if possible.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: I'll just check.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: I'm sorry, Tom.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: It's already booked that week.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: It's free the week beginning the 28th though, for seven nights.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY
audioscript.explain: Q1: Tom first asks for the week beginning the **14th**, but Shirley says *'It's already booked that week'*. She then offers *'the week beginning the 28th'* as the only free time in May. So the available date is the **28th**.

audioscript.text: In fact, that's the only time you could have it in May.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: Oh, well, we could manage that, I think.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: We'd just need to change a couple of things.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: How much would it cost?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: That's the beginning of high season, so it'd be £550 for the week.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY
audioscript.explain: Q2: Shirley explains that the 28th is *'the beginning of high season'*, so the price is higher. She directly states the cost: *'it'd be £550 for the week'*. So the answer is **550**.

audioscript.text: Ah, that's a bit more than we wanted to pay, I'm afraid.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: We've budgeted up to £500 for accommodation.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Well, we've just finished converting another building into a cottage,
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: which we're calling Chervil Cottage.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY
audioscript.explain: Q3: Shirley mentions a new, cheaper cottage and says *'we're calling it Chervil Cottage'*. She then spells it out: *'C H E R, V for Victor, I L'*. So the name is **Chervil**.

audioscript.text: Sorry? what was that again?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Chervil. C H E R, V for Victor, I L.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: Oh, that's a herb, isn't it?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: It grows fairly wild around here.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: You could have that for the week you want for £480.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: OK, so could you tell me something about it, please?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Of course.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: The building was built as a garage.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY
audioscript.explain: Q4: When describing the new cottage's history, Shirley says *'The building was built as a garage'*. **'Built as'** means its original purpose. So the answer is **garage**.

audioscript.text: It's a little smaller than Granary Cottage.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: So that must sleep two people as well.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: There's a double bedroom.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: Does it have a garden?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Yes, you get to it from the living room through French doors.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY
audioscript.explain: Q5: Tom asks *'Does it have a garden?'* and Shirley replies *'Yes'*. She adds that you get to **it** from the living room through French doors — **'it'** refers to the **garden**. So the answer is **garden**.

audioscript.text: And we provide two deck chairs.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: We hope to build a patio in the near future, but I wouldn't like to guarantee it'll be finished by May.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: OK.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: The front door opens onto the old farmyard, and parking isn't a problem.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: There's plenty of room at the front for that.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY
audioscript.explain: Q6: Shirley says *'parking isn't a problem'* and explains there is *'plenty of room at the front for that'*. **'That'** refers back to **parking**. So the answer is **parking**.

audioscript.text: There are some trees and potted plants there.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: What about facilities in the cottage?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: It has standard things like a cooker and fridge, I presume.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: In the kitchen area, there's a fridge freezer.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: And we've just put in an electric cooker.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: Is there a washing machine?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Yes, there's also a TV in the living room which plays DVDs too.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: The bathroom is too small for a bath, so there's a shower instead.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: I think a lot of people prefer that nowadays anyway.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: It's more environmentally friendly, isn't it?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Unless you spend half the day in it.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Exactly.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: What about heating?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: It sometimes gets quite cool at that time of year.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: There's central heating, and if you want to light a fire, there's a stove.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: We can provide all the wood you need for it.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY
audioscript.explain: Q7: Shirley talks about a stove for a fire and says *'We can provide all the wood you need for it'*. The stove burns this **wood** to make the room cozy. So the answer is **wood**.

audioscript.text: It smells so much nicer than coal, and it makes the room very cozy.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: We've got one in our own house.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: That sounds very pleasant.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Perhaps we should come in the winter to make the most of it.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Yes, we find we don't want to go out when we've got the fire burning.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: There are some attractive views from the cottage which I haven't mentioned.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: There's a famous stone bridge, it's one of the oldest in the region, and you can see it from the living room.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY
audioscript.explain: Q8: Shirley describes a view from the living room: *'There's a famous stone bridge... you can see it'*. The question asks for the view, which is the old **bridge**. So the answer is **bridge**.

audioscript.text: It isn't far away.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: The bedroom window looks in the opposite direction, and has a lovely view of the hills, and the Monument at the top.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY
audioscript.explain: Q9: For the bedroom view, Shirley says you can see *'the hills, and the Monument at the top'*. The question asks for the hilltop view, which is the **Monument**. So the answer is **monument**.

audioscript.text: Well, uh, that all sounds perfect.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: I'd like to book it, please.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Would you want a deposit?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Yes, we ask for 30% to secure your booking.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: So that'll be, um, £144.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: And when would you like the rest of the money?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: You're coming in May, so the last day of March, please.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY
audioscript.explain: Q10: Shirley asks for the final payment by a specific date: *'the last day of March, please'*. The question asks for the deadline, which is the end of **March**. So the answer is **March**.

audioscript.text: Fine.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Excellent.
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: Could I just take your details so that I can...
audioscript.speaker: SHIRLEY

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER
